title: Notice pay vs garden leave - what employment contracts often get wrong
p1:
Many employees and employers think notice pay and garden leave mean the same thing.

They don’t — and that small difference can create big problems.
p2:
A common mistake in employment contracts is treating garden leave as simply “paying someone not to work.”

Notice pay usually means the employee leaves and receives payment for the notice period. Garden leave means the employee remains employed but is asked not to work, often to protect confidential information or business relationships.
p3:
The surprising part? During garden leave, the employee may still owe duties to the employer because the employment relationship continues.

A well-drafted contract should clearly explain what happens during this period, including restrictions, benefits, and responsibilities.

The practical lesson: unclear wording can create disputes when a company wants protection and an employee wants clarity.
conclusion: Have you seen an employment contract that clearly explained garden leave, or was the difference between notice pay and garden leave left unclear?
